newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS-Worse seen for sagging US sour crude market.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Worse seen for sagging US sour crude market.

text.p: The sagging sour crude oil market in the U.S. will get worse as mushrooming supply at home and abroad meets languishing domestic demand, industry analysts and traders say.

Rising availabilities from Mexico, Venezuela, Canada and the U.S. Gulf of Mexico, as well as possible sales of Iraqi crude into the region, have changed the structure of the U.S. sour crude market, pushing prices to a new, lower range.
"I think you'll see the sweet/sour differential widen further," says one Gulf Coast refiner who buys sour crude. "That spells doom and gloom for sour producers."
Higher in sulfur than sweet crude, sour crude requires extra processing to churn out refined products and generally fetches a lower market price.

The spread between bellwether West Texas Intermediate/Cushing and West Texas Sour/Midland averaged $1.66 a barrel in January 1997, compared to 90 cents a barrel in January 1996 and just 56 cents 10 years ago. WTS/Midland has slumped to around $2.85 below WTI/Cushing at the end of last week.
Mexico's climbing production of Maya crude, a heavy crude with a sulfur content of 3.4 percent, highlights the burgeoning supply trend in the region.
State-owned Pemex produced 1.4 million barrels per day (bpd) of Maya last December, up 10.4 percent from a year earlier.
Similarly, Maya exports averaged 833,000 bpd in December 1995, up seven percent from a year ago, according to Pemex. The bulk of Pemex's exports land in the United States.
Maya accounts for about half of Mexico's total crude output, which averaged 2.86 million bpd last year. Output is targeted to reach an average of 3.08 million bpd in 1997.
Meanwhile, Venezuela's dizzying rise in crude production, much of which is heavy and sour, has exacerbated the fundamental weakness of U.S. sour crude.

State-owned Petroleos de Venezuela forecasts that total production capacity will soar to 6.3 million bpd in 2006 from 3.4 million bpd in 1996. Like Mexico, the U.S. swallows up most of the Venezuela's exports.
Sour crude looks just as abundant closer to home.

"Canadian crude production is increasing quite significantly...but refiners in Canada aren't increasing their throughputs significantly," says Steven Kelly, associate consultant with Purvin & Gertz in Calgary.

Canadian supplies of heavy sour crude, including wellhead and blended flows, averaged an estimated 659,000 bpd in 1996, up from 622,000 in 1995. The forecast for 1997 is 747,000 bpd, according to Houston-based Purvin & Gertz.
While Canadian output is climbing and refinery demand is sluggish, pipeline capacity into the U.S. has expanded, unleashing even more sour crude into the U.S. market.

Yet another mounting source of sour crudes are new deep-water fields in the Gulf of Mexico. Major oil companies such as Royal Dutch/Shell and British Petroleum, armed with new exploration and production technologies, are venturing into ever-greater depths where most of the reserves are sour.

Short-term factors, such as refinery turnarounds, shutdowns and refiners' normal seasonal shift to sweeter crudes in preparation for the summer driving seasion, have undercut sour crudes even further.
On the U.S. West Coast, for example, the shutdown of a hydrocracking unit at Tosco's refinery in Martinez, California has backed more heavy sour crude into the U.S. market.

The 32,000 bpd hydrocracker, which turns fuel oil into gasoline, has been down since an explosion and fire on January 21. Since then, Tosco has declared force majeure on near-term purchases of heavy crude, which total about 40,000 bpd for the Martinez plant.
Efforts to sell Iraqi crude into the U.S. Gulf Coast add to sour crudes' dim prospects.

"Supplies are generally rising to outpace demand, and now you have the situation of Iraq trying to shove more crude into the market," says William Brown, president of New York-based W.H. Brown & Co. "It's a supply-driven phenomenon."
U.S. trading company Bayoil recently postponed a possible U.S. shipment of Iraqi Basrah Light crude from March into April after failing to elicit buyer interest.
--New York Energy Desk ((+1 212 859 1620))
